cards.title: Concepts of History
body: The term history is derived from a Greek word historia, meaning inquiry. Even though it is defined as the study of past developments, it also studies the present and predicts for the future. To create this record, historians use sources such as documents, artifacts and artworks.
The historical period began from 5000-6000 years ago, when people first began to write and keep records. The period before written records is called prehistory.

cards.title: Model answer: what is history?
cards.problem: (Short answer) Define history and explain how historians know about the past.

steps.text: Start with the word: "history" comes from the Greek word *historia*, meaning inquiry.
Give the definition: history studies past human developments, and it also helps us understand the present and think about the future.
Name the evidence: historians use sources such as documents, artifacts and artworks.
Add the time frame: the historical period began 5000–6000 years ago when people began to write; the time before written records is prehistory.

cards.answer: History (from Greek *historia*, inquiry) is the study of the human past, based on sources such as documents, artifacts and artworks; it began with writing 5000–6000 years ago – before that is prehistory.

lessons.title: Significance of the Study of History

cards.title: Significance of the Study of History
body: History is a necessity because no society can get along without knowledge of its history. History is to the society, as memory is to the individual. History helps us to:
Learn about the politics, economy and culture of different people.
Draw lessons from previous human experiences so as not to repeat past mistakes.
Be conscious of the variety of our heritages and preserve the good ones.
Be proud of our cultural and national identity. 1.2 Prehistory
The entire span of human history is divided into two periods: prehistory and history.

The prehistoric period was the era before writing was developed. Since Historians rely on written records to write history of the past and no written records exist for the prehistory of humankind, the field that studies this period is known as Archaeology.

Archaeology is the study of past societies through an analysis of what people have left behind, examining dug up and examine artifacts such as tools, pottery, paintings, weapons, buildings, and fossil remains.
During the prehistoric period, the following three key developments took place:
The first humans, Homo sapiens, originated in Africa after a lengthy process of evolution.
Humans began to migrate out of Africa before 1000 years and settled first the Euro Asian land Australia and the Americas.
Humans begin to develop ‘culture.’ 1.3 Sources of History
A source is the material out of which history is written, no history can be written without a source. Generally, sources of history are classified into two types, primary and secondary.

Primary sources come directly from the actual period of the past including letters, diaries, tax rolls, treaties, tools, clothing, artifacts, graves, paintings, archeological remains, recordings, photographs, magazines, newspapers, archives, eyewitness accounts on both past and present and information from mass media. Primary sources also include firsthand account of an event documented later, such as biographies, memoirs and oral traditions.

Secondary sources are accounts of a particular period in history written later by someone who did not participate in the events; including published and unpublished works such as books, articles, theses and dissertations (research papers).
Forms of sources; both primary and secondary sources are found in different forms.
A) Written Sources; could be published or unpublished materials or anything recorded on stones, bones, papyrus reeds, paper and Information Technology (IT) products.
B) Material Sources include archaeological, historical and contemporary goods, items and artifacts reflecting the material culture of society.

C) Oral Sources; There are three types of oral sources 1. Eyewitness accounts: are descriptions of the details of an event or events given by someone who saw or participated in them. 2. Rumors: are unconfirmed accounts or explanations of events transmitted by word of mouth. Rumors function as sources of history because they provide some picture of the thinking, perception, wishes and fears of a society or groups within it. 3. Oral Traditions: are cultural and traditional accounts transmitted orally from one generation to another in speech or song, and may take the form of folktales, sayings, ballads, songs or chants.

Sources themselves are not sufficient to produce history. First, they must always be checked and crosschecked before they are used in historical writing and must not be taken as final. 1.4 Dating Time in History
History can’t be written or can’t be known without the knowledge of the time when events occurred. There are various methods of measuring time, but generally dating methods are classified into two:
Relative and Actual. Relative dating method does not give us the precise time, but actual does. Relative dating measures time in terms of a decade, century and millennium.

The Calendar system helps measure and record time. The Babylonians were probably the first people to develop a calendar, their lunar calendar had 12 months of 30 days each. The Egyptians used a solar calendar with 365 days, divided into 12 months of 30 days each and 5 extra days at the end. In ancient Greece, a unipolar calendar (a combination of solar and lunar calendar), with 354 days was used.

Roman emperor, Julius Caesar, introduced a solar calendar with 365 days and 366 days at leap year. This calendar had the same number of days as the Gregorian calendar. Modern calendars used today include the Gregorian, Julian, the Hebrew, Islamic Calendar (Hegira), Geez and the Chinese Calendars. The Gregorian is the most widely used one throughout the world.

cards.title: Model answer: primary and secondary sources
cards.problem: (Exam question) Distinguish between primary and secondary sources of history and give two examples of each.

steps.text: Define a source: the material out of which history is written – no history without a source.
Primary sources come directly from the period itself: letters, diaries, treaties, tools, graves, photographs, eyewitness accounts (also memoirs and oral traditions).
Secondary sources are written later by people who did not take part: books, articles, theses and dissertations.
Conclude: a diary of a soldier is primary; a textbook chapter about the war is secondary.

cards.answer: Primary sources date from the time of the event (e.g. letters, treaties, artifacts, eyewitness accounts); secondary sources are later accounts by non-participants (e.g. books, articles, theses).

cards.title: Dating Artifacts and Fossils
body: One of the most important and difficult jobs of archaeologists is dating their finds because determining the age of human fossils makes it possible to understand when and where the first humans emerged. Likewise, the dating of artifacts left by humans helps scientists understand the growth of early societies.
Radiocarbon and Potassium-Argon dating methods are the two most often used dating methods. 1.5 Cause and Effect

Since societies change over time and no society remains static or stagnant, the history of society is the history of change. There are two important components in the process of change: cause and effect.

A Cause is something that makes an event or an action happen or exist while an effect is the result or outcome of an action or an event. Historians use cause and effect analyses to find the reason for what happened in the past. 1.6 Chronology
Chronology is a sequence of events based on the time of occurrence. Writing history is just like building a house. Likewise, the events of history should be carefully studied sequentially.

cards.title: 2.1 Human Evolution and the Paleolithic Age
body: There are 3 stages of Human Evolution;

The First Hominids- According to the scientific theory of evolution, the earliest humanlike creatures known as Australopithecines lived in Africa as long as three to four million years ago. They were the first hominids (humans and other creatures that walk upright), make simple stone tools and resemble modern humans, but had smaller brain capacities.

Homo erectus- A second stage in early human evolution occurred with the appearance of Homo erectus (“upright human being”) around 1.5 million years ago. They had relatively bigger brains and used stone tools and fire to keep warm in colder areas. They gathered wild plants and hunted animals. Since hunting large animals required organization and communication, they formed small groups for protection, the provision of food, and religious rituals.

Homo sapiens- the third stage is characterized by the emergence of Homo sapiens (“man the thinker”) 250,000 years ago. Homo sapiens gave rise to two distinct subgroups; Neanderthals and Homo sapiens sapiens.

Neanderthals- their fossils were first found in the Neander valley in Germany. They flourished between 100,000-30,000 B.C.E. in Europe and Southwest Asia. They lived in both caves and open air sites, used a variety of stone tools and fire, hunted mammals and made clothes from the skins of animals. They were also the first early people to bury their dead and this shows a belief in life after death. By around 30,000 B.C.E., the Neanderthals disappeared for reasons still unknown.

The Homo sapiens- were the first anatomically modern humans (people like us). They appeared in Africa between 200,000 -150,000 years ago and began to spread outside Africa around 100,000 years ago in a slow process that populated almost every corner of the globe by 10,000 B.C.E. The Paleolithic Age (2,500,000 -10,000) and the Hunting-Gathering Communities
The term Paleolithic is derived from Greek, meaning “old stone”, thus the Paleolithic Age is sometimes called the Old Stone Age because of the extensive use of stone tools.

Lifestyle- Paleolithic people relied on hunting and gathering for their daily food. They gathered wild nuts, fruits, grains, and green plants; and they hunted various animals, including buffalo, horses, bison, and reindeer. In coastal areas depended on fishing as their main source of food.

Tools- Over the years, Paleolithic people developed better stone tools. They developed the hand ax, to chop, cut, scrape, and dig holes. They also invented the spear, and later the bow and arrow, which made hunting much easier. They also made harpoons and fishhooks from bones to increase their catch of fish.

Shelter- those who lived in cold climates, found shelter in caves. Over time, they created new types of shelter with a simple structure of wood sticks or bones of large animals covered with animal hides.
Fire- was first used by the Homo erectus for protection from wild animals, cooking food and to keep warm.

Art- existed mostly in the form of cave paintings of large animals by using red, yellow, and black paints made from crushed mineral ores and animal fats. They used their fingertips, crushed twigs and even brushes made with animal hairs.

Social organization- Paleolithic people formed into bands of twenty or thirty where women did most of the gathering and men hunted. Both men and women played roles in providing food, there was equality between them. 2.2 The Agricultural (Neolithic) Revolution 8000-4000 B.C.E

The word Neolithic is Greek for “new stone” even though the biggest change that occurred in this age was the shift from hunting-gathering lifestyle to agriculture and domestication of animals, providing regular supply of food.

Spread of Agriculture- Agriculture probably originated in the highlands of the Middle East. It was then adapted to the valleys of Tigris and Euphrates rivers in southwestern Asia and eastern Asia Minor, Mesoamerica (Central America), western Africa, southeastern Asia, China, and the Andes. Consequences of the Neolithic Revolution

The beginning of settled life- because of agriculture, people settled and begun to build houses. This marked the emergence of Neolithic villages in southwest Asia, India, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica.
The emergence of trade – due to agriculture, surplus food was produced encouraging the rise of trade.
The development of division of labor -people begun to do other things besides farming, some specialized in crafts and others in art.
The Refinement of stone tools and cloth making- artisans began making refined tools, blades and sickles while clothes were woven from cotton and plant fibers.

steps.text: Stage 1 – Australopithecines: the first hominids, in Africa 3–4 million years ago; walked upright, made simple stone tools, small brains.
Stage 2 – Homo erectus ("upright human being"), about 1.5 million years ago: bigger brains, used stone tools and fire, lived in small groups, hunted and gathered.

cards.title: Impact of Geography on Mesopotamian Civilization
body: Mesopotamia means “the land between the rivers” because of its location between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers of the Fertile Crescent (stretching from the Mediterranean Sea to the Persian Gulf) in present day Iraq.

The area had little rain fall, but had fertile soil enriched by layers of silt deposited by the two rivers. They introduced irrigation to control the irregular flow of the rivers and use it for farming.
Ancient Mesopotamia includes three important areas: Sumer, Akkad, and Assyria. 1.The Sumerian City

Even though their origin is still unknown, they had established a number of independent city-states in southern Mesopotamia and eventually expanded into their neighbors by 3000 B.C.E. These city-states were the basic units of Sumerian civilization.

Sumerian cities- were surrounded by walls included small houses for peasants and the larger ones for officials, priests and priestesses. Since Mesopotamia had little stone or wood, they used sun-dried mud bricks for construction.

Economy- Their economy was based chiefly on farming, but eventually trade and industry also became important as they were well known for their metal works, woolen textiles, and pottery. They imported copper, tin, and timber; and exported dried fish, wool, crops, and metal goods. Sumerian traders travelled by land to the eastern Mediterranean and by sea to India. The invention of the wheel around 3000 B.C.E. led to wheeled carts, which made the transport of goods easier.

Social Structure- their city-states contained three major social classes: nobles, commoners, and slaves. Nobles included royals and priestly officials. Commoners were those who worked as farmers, merchants, fishers, and craftspeople, majority of Sumerians were farmers. Slaves belonged to palace officials, who used them mostly in building projects while temple officials used female slaves to weave cloth and grind grain. Rich landowners also used slaves to farm their lands.

Government-In the early stages of the city-states, priests and priestesses played an important role in governing the people until the power was eventually passed onto the kings. Sumerians believed that kings derived their power from the gods and were agents of the gods. The kings organized an army and irrigation projects, and supervised the building of public works.

Religion- Environmental conditions such as violent river floods, strong winds and famines made the Mesopotamians think that this world was controlled by gods and goddesses. They were polytheistic (believed in many gods) as they worshipped almost 3000 gods and goddesses. Temples were the most important and wealthy buildings as they were dedicated to the chief god or goddess of the city, built on the top of a rectangular tower called a ziggurat. The Sumerians believed that gods and goddesses owned and ruled the cities.

Writing- their greatest invention was writing. Around 3000 B.C.E. they created a Cuneiform (“wedge-shaped”) system of writing marks on clay tablets baked or dried in the sun. Once dried, these tablets lasted a very long time.

Inventions- they invented several tools and devices that made their daily life easier and more productive such as, the wagon wheel for transportation, potter’s wheel to shape containers and the sundial to keep time. They were the first people to make bronze out of copper and tin.
They also made remarkable achievements in Mathematics and Astronomy. Mesopotamian astronomers developed a 12-month calendar based on the movements of the moon.

Empires in Ancient Mesopotamia- the growth of new Sumerian city-states grew led to conflicts. The city-states began to fight each other for control of land and water among themselves and were also exposed to invasions by foreign forces.

cards.title: 2. Akkadian Empire
body: The Akkadians were Semitic people located north of the Sumerian cities. In around 2340 B.C.E., their leader Sargon invaded the Sumerian city-states and set up the first empire in world history by uniting Mesopotamia with his lands along the Mediterranean cost. An empire is a large state usually headed by an emperor or empress.
The Akkadian Empire begun to decline after 300 years of prosperity in 2100 B.C.E after it was attacked by its neighbors. The Empire remained in a state of chaos and conflict until 1792 B.C.E.

The Reign of Hammurabi (1792-1750) - Sumer and Akkad were united into a new Mesopotamian Empire in 1792 B.C.E under Hammurabi of Babylon (a city-state south of Akkad). He was a successful military leader and administrator and best remembered for his law code (a collection of 282 laws).

Hammurabi’s laws were based on the following two legal ideas: 1. Criminals should be punished severely. But punishments varied according to the social class of the victim. 2. Equal retaliation for a crime committed (“an eye for an eye, tooth for a tooth”).

Hammurabi’s law code covered almost every aspect of people’s lives, contained laws of property, trade, family and labor. The empire declined after Hammurabi’s death because his successors were unable to protect it.

cards.title: Impact of Geography
body: The Nile is the longest river in the world extending for more than 6,346 Kms starting from the highlands of Ethiopia and countries of the Great Lakes region (Burundi, Tanzania, Rwanda, and Uganda). It splits into 2 branches before joining the Mediterranean Sea forming the triangular- shaped Nile Delta.
Ancient Egypt’s important cities developed at the tip of the Nile Delta. The land north of the Delta was called Lower Egypt while the land south of the Nile Delta was called Upper Egypt.

cards.title: Emergence of Egyptian Civilization
body: In about 3100 B.C.E., King Menes united upper and lower Egypt into a single kingdom with Memphis (a city where Upper and Lower Egypt met) as its capital.

Egyptian history is divided into three major periods, known as the Old Kingdom, Middle Kingdom, and the New Kingdom and were marked by strong leadership, peace, building of temples and pyramids, and strong intellectual and cultural activities. Intermediate periods were the years between the three Kingdoms, and were marked by wars, external invasions, and decline in building activities.

cards.title: The Old Kingdom (2700 to 2200 B.C.E)
body: The Old Kingdom was a period of prosperity and peace under powerful kings. Pharaoh (the great house) was the title given to the king, they were believed to be gods. From ancient times, the Nile was referred to as the “gift of the Nile” because it is the source of life in Egypt. The River had two important contributions in Egyptian history; One, it enabled Egyptian farmers to grow surplus food, and two; it united Egypt by making both transportation and communication within Egypt easier.

The Egyptian civilization gained the protection from external invasions ensuring its continuation for over a thousand years thanks to its natural barriers, including the deserts to the east and west of the Nile, the Red Sea to the east, the cataracts (rapids) to the south, and the Mediterranean Sea to the north.

Pyramids- were one of the greatest achievements of Egyptian civilization, Pyramid building begun during the Old Kingdom. They were used for the Pharaoh’s burial, while smaller pyramids were used for his family and mastabas (rectangular buildings) were used as the burials for the pharaoh’s officials). They believed that humans had physical and spiritual parts. Preserving the physical body of the dead person in the tomb filled with all the necessities of daily life meant that the spiritual part of the dead person could return and continue its life after death.
The pyramids were also symbols of power and glory.

Mummification is a process by which a dead body was preserved in order to prevent it from rotting. This process was done by priests who first removed the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines and placed them in four jars. Then they removed the brain through the nose and covered the corpse with salt in order to absorb the body’s water.

The biggest pyramid was built under King Khufu in around 2540 B.C.E at Giza and according to Herodotus (a Greek historian), it took 100,000 Egyptians twenty 20 years to build the Great Pyramid. The pyramid is guarded by a huge rock statue of the great Sphinx (a creature with a lion’s body and a head of a human).

cards.title: Middle Kingdom (2050 to 1652)
body: The collapse of the Old Kingdom was followed by 150 years of chaos until a new pharaoh restored stability and created the Middle Kingdom. The Middle Kingdom is considered as the Golden Age because Egypt began to expand by conquering Nubia (located south of Egypt), it also sent armies into Syria and Palestine.
Trade also begun with Mesopotamia, Nubia, Crete and Syria, while begun a public projects such as draining of swampland and construction of canals.

cards.title: The New Kingdom (1567 to 1085 B.C.E)
body: The Middle Kingdom ended with the invasion of the Hyksos from Western Asia in 1652 B.C.E. The Hyksos used horse-drawn war chariots and defeated the Egyptian soldiers who used donkey carts.

Egyptians learned making bronze tools and weapons, horse- drawn war chariots from the Hyksos and used the new weapons to defeat the Hyksos after a 100 year rule and reunite Egypt marking the beginning of the New Kingdom.

During the period of the New Kingdom, Egypt created an empire and became the most powerful state in Mediterranean world after occupying Syria, Palestine, and Libya. Egyptian pharaohs built many new temples, for example, the first woman pharaoh, Hatshepsut, built a great temple at Deir el Bahri, near Thebes. The land of Punt (Eritrean Red Sea coast) was first mentioned in this Temple.
The New Kingdom collapsed in 1085 B.C.E due to internal conflicts and external invasions. For the next 1000 years, Egypt was dominated by Libyans, Nubians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans.

Egyptian Economy- most Egyptians were peasants and depended on the Nile valley for farming, and produced wheat, barley, beans, and cotton. Trade and commerce were also important parts of the Egyptian economy; they traded with Sumer, Phoenicia, Syria, Crete, Nubia and the Land of Punt. They exported mainly grains, big stones, and cotton. And imported wood, elephants, animal skins, and precious stones.

Moreover, some Egyptians were engaged in crafts, Egyptian artisans made an incredible variety of goods such as stone dishes; painted boxes; wooden furniture; gold, silver, and copper tools; paper and rope made of papyrus; and linen clothes.

Social Structure- Egyptian society was organized like a pyramid, with the pharaoh, the nobles and priests at the top forming the upper class of the society. The Middle class included merchants, artisans, scribes, and tax collectors, while the lower class was composed of peasants and slaves. The peasants paid taxes in the form of crops to the upper class, provided military services and were forced into labor for building projects.
Women had a relatively good status in the Egyptian society. They could own and inherit property, operate businesses while upper class women could become priestesses, and four queens became pharaohs.

Government- The pharaohs had an unlimited power to rule their people. During the Old Kingdom, the pharaohs established a government bureaucracy (an administrative organization with officials and regular procedures) headed by an official known as Vizier. Egypt was divided into provinces run by governors appointed by the pharaoh.

Religion- since they were polytheistic, many of their gods were associated with heavenly bodies and natural forces. The sun, land and river gods were the most important gods because the sun, the land and the river were vital to their lives. The sun god was known as “Re”, the river god “Osiris”, and the land god “Isis”.

Writing and Education- Egyptian writing system is called Hieroglyphics, meaning “priest carvings” or “sacred writings” in Greek, it emerged around 3000 B.C.E. The system used pictures to represent objects, sound or ideas carved in stone before the invention of paper (papyrus). Scribes mastered hieroglyphic writing and taught upper class boys from the age of 10.

Schools were first established to train priests to read, write, arithmetic and religious ceremonies but as the Egyptian civilization grew; temple schools became the only centers of general education. The temple of the Sun god at Heliopolis was a famous center of learning.
Art and Science- Egyptians architectural included pyramids, temples, and monuments which depended on their knowledge of Mathematics and Geometry to calculate area and volume.

The Egyptians also developed an accurate 365-day calendar based on the flooding of the Nile. Moreover, the Egyptians made important advances in medicine. Egyptian doctors used to treat bone fractures, wounds, dental and internal cases. They even practiced elementary form of spinal surgeries.

cards.title: Impact of Geography
body: Nubia is located south of Egypt crisscrossed by the first cataract of the Nile and the confluence of the blue and white Nile. Nubia became an important trade point between Egypt and the Mediterranean region on the one hand, and the interior of Africa and the Red Sea on the other. Nubia was rich in rainfall and minerals, especially iron ore.

cards.title: Emergence of Nubian Civilization
body: Egyptian Rule- trade between Nubia and Egypt begun during Old Kingdom of Egypt and the Kerma kingdom of Nubia that emerged in 2000 B.C.E. But during the beginning of the New Kingdom (1500 B.C.E), Nubia fell under the direct rule of Egypt with the objective of controlling trade. During the 500 years of Egyptian rule, towns and temples of Egyptians style were built in Nubia. Also, Nubians copied Egyptian religion, language and writing.

The Kingdom of Kush- Egypt declined due to internal conflicts and external invasions resulting in its withdrawal from Nubia, providing Nubian rulers a chance to establish the independent state of Kush in about 1000 B.C.E.

Kushite Rule of Egypt- the kings of Kush grew very powerful under the Egyptian model of government and administration. In 750 B.C., the Kush conquered Egypt and ruled for almost 60 years until the Assyrian invasion of Egypt in 670 B.C.E. The Assyrian invasion of Egypt forced the Kushites to withdraw.

Napata was the capital of the Kush until it was moved south wards into Meroe because of two reasons; Meroe was rich in iron ore, timber, rainfall and its location was favorable for trade. The kingdom reached the height of its power and remained until the 4th century C.E.

Economy- was primarily based on farming using the Nile and rainfall to grow sorghum and millet. The second most important economic activity of the Nubians was its extensive trade with Egypt, India, Arabia, and later with the Roman Empire. They exported ivory, gold, ebony, slaves and iron products in exchange for luxury goods such as jewelry, fine cotton cloth, silver lamps, and glass bottles. In addition to agriculture and trade, iron manufacturing and animal husbandry were also important.

Social Structure and Government- The royal family, the nobility, and the priests formed the upper class, below them were artisans and traders, while the peasants constituted the lower class. Nubian kings had absolute power and they were chosen from a single family and approved by the nobility and priests. The mother of the king was an important figure in the government; she helped to maintain stability and smooth transition from one reign to the next.

Religion and Writing System- the culture, language, religion and writing system of the Nubians were highly influenced by Egypt thus Egyptian hieroglyphics, gods and Pyramids were widely used in Nubia.

The Nubians gradually developed their own culture; Meroitic language replaced Egyptian language while Hieroglyphics was replaced by a new writing system. Meroitic language is related to the language of the Nara in Eritrea. The Nubians were polytheistic and worshipped Egyptian gods along with their own local gods.

Art and Architecture- were heavily influenced by Egypt until the Nubians developed their own distinct art and architecture. They drew pictures, engravings, and statues of tropical animals such as lion, ostrich, giraffe, and elephant. They produced pottery and built pyramids long after pyramid-building had stopped in Egypt.
Decline- Its collapsed in 350 C.E. due to a number of factors such as; the decline of agriculture, iron industry, and foreign trade and Aksumite invasion of Meroe under King Ezana.

cards.title: Impact of Geography
body: Phoenicia is a narrow strip of land along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea in present day Lebanon. Phoenicia was made up of a group of city-states such as; Byblos, Sidon, Tyre, Beirut (all found in present day Lebanon) and Carthage (modern Tunisia).

Phoenicians were Semitic speaking people and were essentially called “people of the sea.” Because they depended on the Mediterranean Sea for their livelihood. They were famous seafarers, traders and ship builders. Also, the temperate climate of the Mediterranean region helped them to grow crops such as wheat, grapes and date palms. Emergence of Phoenician Civilization

The first settlements were along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea in around 2500 B.C.E. For almost a thousand years, they were under the control of Egypt until they became independent after Egypt begun to decline in around 1200 B.C.E. They expanded their trade and became powerful in the Mediterranean Sea. By the end of the 9th century B.C.E., the Phoenicians had founded many colonies in North Africa, Spain and Sardinia.

Economy- the primary economic activity was trade with Phoenician cities such as Byblos, Tyre, Sidon, and Carthage became trading centers on the coasts of Mediterranean Sea and reached the Atlantic Ocean, Britain and the western coasts of Africa. The Phoenicians produced a number of goods for foreign markets, including purple dye, glass, and lumber. Agriculture was the second economic activity because of its fertile soil and the Mediterranean climate, they grew wheat, grapes, figs, and date palms. In addition to trade and agriculture, they also manufactured purple dye (a dye used for decorating clothes and pottery), weaving, glass making, metal and ivory works,
Religion and Government- Phoenicians were polytheistic; each city-state had its own chief god. The Phoenician religious system was a combination of their own and that of Egypt and Greece.
They were ruled by hereditary kings (Monarchs) assisted by nobles but later changed from to republics, i.e., from polities ruled by hereditary kings to polities ruled by elected leaders and a senate.

Writing System- their most important contribution to human kind was the development of alphabets. The Phoenician alphabets had 22 letters, each of which represented a distinct sound and was used to spell the words in their language. Unlike the Egyptian and Mesopotamian systems, Phoenician alphabets were not pictographic. This alphabet system was passed on to the Greeks and the Romans giving birth to the modern Alphabets used today.

cards.title: The Rise of Assyrian Empire
body: After the decline of the Egyptian civilization in 13th B.C.E, the Hittite and Hebrew kingdoms appeared on the borders of Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilizations. But these kingdoms collapsed, and were replaced by the Assyrian and Persian Empires.

The Assyrian Empire was established by Semitic speaking people in 700 B.C.E after the fall of the Hittite and Hebrew kingdoms, with its capital at Nineveh. The Assyrians were masters of iron weapons. The Empire included Mesopotamia, parts of the Iranian Plateau, sections of Asia Minor, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt. But was weakened due to internal conflicts in 612 B.C.E., and fell to a coalition of Chaldeans and Medes (people who lived in the East).

Economy- Agriculture was the principal basis of Assyrian life, and it depended on rainfall. The second important Assyrian economic activity was trade because of their geographical location, the Assyrians served as intermediaries in the international trade of their time. They mainly exported textiles in exchange for timber, wine, and precious metals and stones.

Social Structure and Religion- 2000 B.C.E, Assyrian society was composed of two groups, free citizens and slaves but by the first millennium B.C.E., however, royal officials constituted the upper class of the free citizens while many peasants lost their land and became serfs. The Assyrians were a relatively open society and mixed with other peoples.

Assyrians were unified by their religion, Assyria means literally, “the land of Ashur,” (the chief god). The king was believed to be the human representative of Ashur. Since the Assyrians considered themselves as guardians of Sumerian and Babylonian culture, many of their religious beliefs were influenced by them. Although they had their own gods most of their gods and goddesses were of Mesopotamian origin.

Government- powerful kings assisted by local officials ruled empire through an efficient system of communication carried by horses, and also established the world’s first libraries at Nineveh under King Ashurbanipal, one of the last Assyrian kings. This library provided abundant information concerning Assyrian and ancient Southwest Asian civilizations.

The Assyrians were good fighters and were renowned for their archery skills, iron weapons, a large , well organized and highly disciplined army composed of an infantry (ground forces) and cavalry (horse mounted troops). The Assyrians used terror in war, they destroyed the lands, dams, looted and destroyed towns, set crops on fire, and cut down trees. The Assyrians were especially known for committing atrocities against their captives.

cards.title: Geography
body: Persia lies at a crossroads between western Asia, the plains of central Asia, the great steppes to the northeast, and Afghanistan and the Indus valley to the east. Persian topography included plateaus, plains, and extensive deserts. Persia was rich in minerals, particularly iron, copper and good rainfall.

cards.title: Emergence and Expansion of the Persian Empire
body: After the collapse of the Assyrian Empire, the Chaldeans, under their king Nebuchadnezzar II, ruled with Babylonia at the center of his Empire. However, the age Chaldean Babylonia was short lived due to Persian invasion in 539 B.C.E.

The Persians were nomadic Indo-European people who lived in modern southwestern Iran, organized in groups until they were united under the Achaemenid dynasty ruled by Cyrus. He created a powerful Persian state that stretched from Asia Minor to western India and ruled from 559 to 530 B.C.E.

In 539 B.C.E. captured Babylon but he treated the Babylonians with wisdom and mercy. That is why the people of his time called him “Cyrus the Great.” and the Medes, Babylonians, and Jews to accepted him as their ruler. He used Assyrian, Babylonian, and Egyptian designs and building methods in building his palaces.

Cyrus’s successors extended the territory of the Persian Empire. His son Cambyses successfully invaded Egypt, while Darius (521-486 B.C) extended the empire to India and Thrace creating the largest empire the world had ever seen. Darius failed to invade Greece because he was defeated at the battle of Marathon in 490 B.C.E

Economy- agriculture was their main economic activity, they grew cereals, legumes, onions, cucumbers, dates, and fruits such as apples, apricots, and pomegranates. The stability of the empire, the use of standard coins and the existence of good trade routes including highways and seaways made long distance trade profitable.

Government- Darius ruled by dividing the Empire into 20 provinces called Satrapies ruled by a Satrap (governor) who collected taxes, provided justice and security, and recruited soldiers for the royal army. In the Empire, the king occupied the highest position because he was believed to have been elected by the Persian god.

The Persian army was composed of many groups of people with 10,000 cavalry and 10,000 infantry forces. Darius created a standing army of professional soldiers because the Empire depended on the military.

Since communication was crucial, roads were built to facilitate transportation, for example, the Royal Road, extended for about 2560 kms. Moreover, a courier service was established with 1000 postal stations along the various roads of the empire.

Social Structure- The early social structure of the Persians was composed of warrior, priestly and peasant classes. They followed a semi-nomadic lifestyle for many years organized into clans. As the Persian Empire grew and became more complex, new groups like tax collectors, administrators, clerks and translators emerged. Majority of Persian society were free citizens who were merchants, craftsmen, and lower ranking government employees. In rural areas, some free peasants owned land while others worked as laborers. Slavery was widely practiced in Persia; they included prisoners of war, rebels, and merchants or artisans who were unable to repay their debts.

Religion- Persians were polytheistic and worshipped powers of nature such as the Sun, Moon, Fire and Wind, but a new religion known as Zoroastrianism was founded by Zoroaster, who wrote his teachings in the Zend Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrianism. It was a monotheistic religion centered on Ahrumazda (the “Wise Lord”). The Fall of the Persian Empire
After Darius, the Persian kings became more and more isolated at their courts; they increased taxes to gain more wealth, loyalty to the empire declined.

Struggles for succession because they Kings had many wives and sons. For example, one king, who ruled in the fourth century B.C.E., had 115 sons, while King Xerxes II reigned for only 45 days before being murdered in bed by his half-brother.
Greek conquest of Persia under Alexander the Great during the 330s B.C.E.

cards.title: Indian Civilization
body: Geography- India is located in Southern Asia. It is sometimes described as a sub-continent because its boundaries separate it from the rest of Asia. Today, the Indian sub-continent divided into two independent countries of India and Pakistan.

Its physical geography includes the Himalaya mountain ranges to the north, Ganges and Indus river valleys to the south and west, Deccan plateau (a dry interior plateau) extending from south of the Ganges to the southern tip of India, and fertile coastal plains in the East and West. Those natural barriers surrounding India have protected it from large-scale invasions for a long period of time.
But a few mountain passes on the northwest border such as the Khyber Pass, enabled some invaders to enter in to northern India. The main feature of India’s climate is the monsoon.

cards.title: Emergence of India’s First Civilization
body: Between 3000 and 1500 B.C.E., a flourishing civilization emerged in the valleys of the Indus River extending hundreds of kilometers from the Himalaya to the coast of the Arabian Sea. Archaeologists have so far discovered the remains of more than a thousand settlements in the valleys of the Indus River, among which are the two cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro. Historians call the civilization which emerged in the Indus River Valleys between 3000 and 1500 B.C.E, Harappan or Indus civilization. The Cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro

At their height, Harappa and Mohenjo-Daro had 35,000 to 40,000 inhabitants. Both cities were carefully planned. The main, broad streets ran in a north-south direction and were crossed by smaller east-west roads. Both cities were divided into large walled neighborhoods, with narrow lanes separating the rows of houses. Houses varied in size, some reaching as high as three stories. Most buildings were constructed of mud bricks baked in ovens and were square. Public wells provided a regular supply of water for all the inhabitants. They had bathrooms with advanced drainage system while wastewater flowed out to drains located under the streets and outside the city through the sewage system. Only a well-organized government could have maintained such carefully structured cities.

Harrapan Rule and Economy- Harappan rulers were believed to have divine right to rule as religion and politics were closely linked. The fact that the royal palace and the holy temple were combined in the fortress at Harappa shows this close connection. Harappan economy was based primarily on farming, the Indus River flooded every year, providing rich soil for the growing of wheat, barley, and peas, the chief crops. The Indus valley civilization also carried on extensive trade with city-states in Mesopotamia through the Persian Gulf.

cards.title: Decline
body: Natural disasters such as floods, earthquake, changes in climate
Decline of agriculture due to the change of the Indus river’s course
Aryan invasion in 1500 B.C.E The Aryan Invasion (1500- 400 B.C.E)

The Aryans were a warrior group of Indo-European nomadic people from central Asia who moved out of their original homeland in central Asia into the plains of northern India in around 1500 B.C.E. They advanced eastward across the Indus and Ganges Valleys and later moved southward into the Deccan Plateau and controlled most of India after conquering the Harappan civilization and creating a new Indian society based on their culture and institutions. Aryan invasion caused the migration of the Dravidians (indigenous people of the Indus valley) further south.

Aryan Economy- the Aryans were pastoralists but they began settled agriculture after settling in India. They grew crops such as wheat, barley, millet, and rice; cotton; and spices such as pepper, ginger, and cinnamon.

Writing System- Like most nomadic peoples, the Aryans had no written language, they only developed their first writing system, known as Sanskrit, in 1000 B.C.E. This enabled them to write down the legends and religious chants and rituals that had previously been passed down orally from generation to generation.

Politics- The early writings of the Aryans show that between 1500 and 400 B.C.E. India was a world of kingdoms and shifting alliances. Aryan princes known as Rajas fought with each other and seized cattle and treasure. New Empires in India

As India under the Aryans was divided into various kingdoms, after 400 B.C.E, it fell victim to invasions from Persia (extending its empire into western India), Greeks and Macedonians led by Alexander the Great. The first Indian dynasty known as Maurya Dynasty emerged after Alexander’s invasion. A. The Mauryan Empire (321- 184 B.C.E)

It was founded by Chandragupta Maurya (324-301 B.C.E.) who established the Mauryan Empire in northern India after driving Alexander out. Being highly centralized, the Empire was divided into provinces ruled by governors appointed by Chandragupta. He had a large army and a secret police because he was afraid of assassinations, food was tasted by servants before he ate it, and he never slept two consecutive nights in the same bed.

The Reign of Asoka- the Mauryan Empire reached its height during the reign of Asoka, the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya. Asoka extended the empire southwards, and ruled almost two-thirds of India. He is considered to be the greatest ruler in the history of India. After conquering two-thirds of India, Asoka converted to Buddhism and began to rule his empire according to the Buddhist religious rules for example; he set up hospitals for both people and animals. He ordered that trees and shelters to be planted along the roads to provide shade for travelers, he sent Buddhist preachers to distant places, he also erected pillars inscribed with Buddhist teachings all over his empire.

Under Asoka, India became the trade center in the region extending from pacific to the Mediterranean. After Asoka’s death in 232 B.C.E., the Mauryan Empire began to decline. The last Mauryan ruler was killed by one of his military commanders in 183 B.C.E.

cards.title: B. The Gupta Empire (320- 535 C.E)
body: Prince Chandragupta (not related to Chandragupta Mauriya) created the Gupta Empire after 500 years of chaos in 320 C.E. The Guptas unified northern India and restored law and order, established a loose control over central India creating the greatest empire in India after the Mauryan Empire.

The Gupta Empire made great achievements in literature, art, mathematics, and science making India the center of learning and spread its culture throughout eastern Asia. Temples were built all over India. As trade was the main source of wealth, the Guptas traded extensively with China, Southeast Asia, and the Mediterranean region. The Gupta period is called India's "Golden Age". In the 6th century C.E., however, the Gupta Dynasty was overthrown by invasions from central Asia.

Society in Ancient India-The conquest by the Aryans had a lasting impact on Indian society. The clash between conquering Aryans and conquered Dravidians created a set of social and class divisions that has lasted in India to the present day known as the Caste system.

The Caste System- was a set of rigid social divisions that determined a person’s occupation and economic potential, and position in society introduced by the Aryans. It was based in part on skin color because the Aryans were light-skinned people and they looked down on the dark- skinned Dravidians, despite the fact that they were much more advanced than the Aryans. There were five major social divisions, known as castes in India
Brahmas or priests- in charge of religious ceremonies highly important in Indian society.
Kshatriyas- warriors.
Vaisyas or commoners- merchants and farmers.
Sudras- peasants and manual laborers and made up a majority of the Indian population.

Untouchables (outcasts) - were not considered human and their presence was considered harmful to others. They were given menial and degrading tasks such as collection of garbage and handling of dead bodies. No Indian would touch or eat food handled by an Untouchable. They lived in separate areas, they were required to tap two sticks together so that others could hear them coming out of their houses and avoid them.

The Family in Ancient India- family was the basic unit of society and it was patriarchal and the eldest male member held legal authority over the family. In this system, only males could inherit property and get education. Divorce was not allowed but a husband could take a second wife, if the first was unable to bear children. In all matters, men dominated women. Perhaps the most telling symbol of women’s dominance by men was the ritual of suttee. In ancient India, the dead were placed on heaps of material called pyres, which were then set on fire. The ritual of suttee required a wife to throw herself on her dead husband’s flaming funeral pyre to die with him.
Indian Religion and Philosophy; One of the greatest contributions of ancient India is its religions, Hinduism and Buddhism. Both of them were developed by the Aryans. I. Hinduism

Originating from the Aryan culture, it developed into a complex religion between 2000 and 1500 B.C.E. There are hundreds of gods and goddesses in Hinduism, but the three chief gods are: Brahma (the Creator), Vishnu (the Preserver) and Siva (the Destroyer).

Reincarnation is one of the basic ideas of Hinduism, it is the belief that a person’s soul is reborn in a different form after death. According to this belief, what people do in their current lives determines what they could be in their next lives. For example, if a person followed a pious life, that person could be reborn in a higher caste than his/her previous caste or if a person followed a sinful life, he/she could be reborn in a lower caste than his/her previous caste or be reborn as an animal. This cycle of rebirth continues until the person becomes completely pure and joins Brahma.

According to Hinduism, people’s place in society and the caste they belong to is determined by god. Since there is nothing people can do to change their caste in current life, they must accept the caste they are born into. Hinduism has created inequality which still survives in Indian society. II. Buddhism

In 6 B.C.E., Buddhism appeared in northern India founded by Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha or the “Enlightened One.” The central idea of Buddhism is that nothing is permanent in the world and no satisfaction can last forever. According to this teaching, man’s suffering is caused by desire and if anybody wants salvation she or he must become a nun or a monk. The most important religious practice of Buddhism is meditation (Yoga).
At the center of Buddha’s teachings is what he called the Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths are:
1. Life is full of suffering
2. Life’s suffering is caused by our desire to satisfy ourselves
3. Life’s suffering can be ended by ending our desire to satisfy ourselves
4. To end our desire to satisfy ourselves we must follow the Eightfold Path, i.e. speaking the truth, not to kill, not to steal…

Buddhism emerged as a reaction and in opposition to Hinduism. But since the latter adopted some of the Buddhist principles, Buddhism gradually disappeared from India. Today Buddhism is practiced mainly in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma, China, Japan, and Indochina.

Indian Literature, Art, and Architecture- The earliest works of Indian literature are the Vedas, passed down orally from generations. With the development of writing, two of India’s great historical poetic epics, the Mahabharata and Ramayana, were written down. Indian art is a reflection of Hindu and Buddhist beliefs. Indian artists were excellent in making human and animal statues, cave temple wall paintings and temples.

Indian Science; Ancient Indians studied astronomy, medicine and mathematics. They studied about revolution of heavenly bodies, had vaccination against smallpox and contributed the number zero, algebra and introduced modern written numbers.

cards.title: Chinese Civilization
body: Geography- surrounded by the Huang He (yellow) and the Chiang Jiang (Yangtze) rivers, China is largest country in Asia surrounded with mountains and deserts isolating it from its neighbors and only 10% of agricultural land.

cards.title: Emergence of Chinese Civilizations
body: The first Chinese Dynasty known as the Xia dynasty was the result of agricultural activities along the fertile river banks of the two rivers.

cards.title: The Shang Dynasty (1750-1045 B.C.E)
body: Replaced the Xia dynasty and ruled the farming society through aristocracy (wealthy upper class people). Their kings were at the top of the society and were buried with their servants in the royal tombs.
The Shang cities were surrounded by huge protective walls and made bronze such as bronze vessels.

cards.title: The Zhou Dynasty (1045-256 B.C.E)
body: Zhou was a Chinese state that rebelled against the Shang dynasty by creating a new dynasty which reigned for 800 years. The Zhou dynasty was ruled by kings assisted by the aristocrats, the kings claimed to have the Mandate of Heaven.

Economy and technology- Irrigation, iron plows, and flood control systems replaced the long adapted rainfall agriculture and increased food production, which in turn led into the increase of population, growth of trade and manufacturing. Silk was the most important trade item exported to central Asia and Greece.

cards.title: Decline
body: China entered ‘the period of Warring States’ from 400-200 B.C as civil wars broke out between the Chinese states due to weak rulers
A new dynasty was created under the Qin or Chin dynasty in 221 B.C.E

cards.title: The Chin (Qin) dynasty (221-206 B.C.E)
body: It was founded by Emperor Qin Shihuangdi who came to power at the age of 13. He created a highly centralized government divided into 3 ministries; Civil service, military, and inspection ministry. There were two levels of administration; provinces and counties. These levels were administered by officials appointed by the emperor based on their skills.

Qin introduced a new single monetary system and road building projects to unite China. He also used harsh laws and policies that severely punished his rivals and forbade books containing different ideas to his.

Shihuangdi begun building the 8000 Kms long Great Wall of China’ to protect China from invasions of the northern nomads, it was finished during the Ming dynasty (14th-15th C). Qin dynasty is also known by the Terra cotta (clay soldiers) buried in Shihuangdi’s tomb.
The dynasty was overthrown after the death of the emperor in 210 B.C because his harsh laws and policies had angered many people.

cards.title: The Han Dynasty (202 B.C-220 C.E)
body: The Han dynasty is one of the greatest dynasties of China, replaced the harsh laws of Qin while preserving the government ministries.
Civil Service examination and a school were set up to train officials based on the teachings of Confucius.
Steel, paper and the water mill were invented, while they developed the skills for iron casting and ship building.
Decline (220 C.E) - central authority declined due to weak and corrupt rulers, peasant revolts, and invasions from the northern nomads putting China into a series of civil wars.

cards.title: Characteristic Features of Chinese Civilization
body: Society- the king and his family were at the top of the society followed by government officials, merchants, artisans, peasants and slaves. Chinese families were headed by males and they had to be obeyed by every member

Religion- the Chinese believed in ancestor worship (the power of the spirits of the dead to do good or bad), thus made offerings and prayers to please them. They buried their kings with slaves and materials because they believed in life after death.

Writing system- the Shangs introduced a simple pictographic writing system written on stones, bones, wood and metal until paper was invented by the Hans enabling the Chinese to produce many books on poetry, literature and philosophy.

Art and Architecture- They used bronze, clay and jade stones to make vases, jewelry and figurines. They built Pagodas (temples), the terra cotta army and the great wall. They were also very good at silk weaving.

Science and Technology- they invented sundials, water clocks, earthquake detectors, a 365 days calendar, magnetic compass, paper, printing and gun powder. They introduced healing methods such as medicines and acupuncture.

cards.title: Chinese Philosophies
body: Confucianism- was founded by Confucius who lived during the Chinese civil war. His ideas were based on the relationships between parents and children, he taught that children should obey their parents; husbands should fulfill their duties and be obeyed by their wives while subjects should be loyal to their kings. He also said that the government should be open to all men with skills. His schools spread all over China after his death.
Taoism- Laozi was a contemporary of Confucius with different ideas. Laozi taught that human beings should accept their lives without trying to improve it.
Legalism- believed that humans are evil by nature and can only be corrected through harsh laws and punishments. Legalists believed on the need for a strong ruler to create peace and keep order.

steps.text: He created a highly centralised government with three ministries: civil service, military and inspection.
Officials were appointed by the emperor on the basis of skill.
He introduced one monetary system and road-building projects to unite the country.
He used harsh laws against rivals and banned books with ideas different from his, and began the Great Wall.

cards.title: Greek Civilization
body: Greek is made up of a small area surrounded by mountain ranges isolated the islands form each other leading in the development of different Greek communities independent from one another. They grew so far apart that they went to war against each other.
The Aegean Sea, Mediterranean Sea, and the black sea were the main source of their livelihood.
The Greek civilization can be divided into six periods
Minoan (2800 to1450 B.C.E)
Mycenaean (1400 to 1100 B.C.E)
Greek Dark Age (1100 to 750 B.C.E)
Archaic (750 to 500 B.C.E)
Classical (500 TO 338 B.C.E)
Hellenistic (323 to 31 B.C.E)

cards.title: 1-2 The Minoan and Mycenaean periods (2800-1100 B.C.E)
body: Was marked by the emergence of complex societies, modern cities, trade and writing system. They both collapsed due to wars and natural disasters putting Greece into a Dark Age.

cards.title: 3. Greece in a Dark Age (1100-750 B.C.E)
body: Following the collapse of the Mycenaean civilization, population and food production declined. But begun once again as Iron tools replaced bronze.
The Greeks adopted Phoenician alphabets and a new writing system with 24 letters. Great poets like Homer emerged.

cards.title: 4. Archaic (Greece after the Dark Age 750-500 B.C.E) – The Emergence of Polis states
body: The Greeks were organized into independent city-states called polis, a town in the countryside. E.g., Athens, Sparta.
An Acropolis was a fortified area in the polis used as a gathering place on which temples and public buildings were built. The Agora was an open marketplace within the polis.
Males were citizens with political rights while women and children were considered as citizens without rights. Slaves and foreign residents were considered as non-citizens.

cards.title: Greek Colonies
body: The Greeks expanded outside their homes looking for farmlands and established new colonies in the coasts of southern Italy and France, eastern Spain, and northern Africa.
They also settled in the coasts of the Black Sea and set up cities such as Byzantium (Constantinople, modern day Istanbul).

cards.title: 5. Classical Greece (500-338 B.C.E)
body: It is marked by the conquest of Macedonian king Philip II, intellectual and cultural growth, and Peloponnesian war.

cards.title: Persian War
body: The Persians occupied Greek cities, but they revolted against the Persians assisted by Athens. Thus, Persian king Darius attacked Athens in 490 B.C but was defeated in the battle of Marathon (42 kms from Athens). The news of the Athenian victory was delivered by Pheidippides.

Darius was replaced by Xerxes, who tried to avenge the Persian defeat by invading Greece in 490 B.C with an army of 180,000, only to be held off by 7000 Greek troops. The Persians were losing until a traitor showed them the way into the center of Greece.
The Greek army defeated the Persians near the Island of Salamis in 479 B.C and after a few months, the Greeks organized a huge army and drove the Persians out.

cards.title: The Peloponnesian War
body: Athens formed a defensive alliance of Greek city-states against the Persians known as the Delian League which later grew into an empire led by Pericles. But they were challenged by Sparta into the Peloponnesian war.
Macedonia emerged as a new power while both Athens and Sparta fought each other.

cards.title: Hellenistic Greece (323-31 B.C.E)
body: Hellenistic is a Greek word meaning, to imitate Greeks.

As the Greek states declined due to civil wars, Macedonia emerged as a strong state under Philip II, who controlled all of Greece. In 336 B.C.E, Philip was replaced by his son Alexander the Great who was taught by Aristotle.

Alexander invaded Turkey, Egypt, Afghanistan, the Persian Empire (327 B.C), Syria, Palestine, Pakistan, and India. He died in Babylon in 323 B.C.E after returning from India, and his empire was divided among his generals.

cards.title: Characteristic Features of Greek Civilization
body: Economy- Farmers grew barely, wheat, grapes, and olives. They practiced seafaring trade with the Middle East, Africa, and Asia and were also engaged in craftsmanship.

Society- It was divided into free people and slaves. Only free native men with land were considered as citizens with political rights while slaves had no right to have families or property. The men provided economic support while the women managed the household.

Government -The expansion of trade brought new wealthy (tyrants) in the city-states who took power from the aristocrats. But by the end of the 6th B.C.E, the rule of tyrants ended allowing the developments of Democracy and Oligarchy. Democracy is a government by the people or the rule of many while Oligarchy is a government dominated by few people.

cards.title: Sparta
body: Sparta was a strong military state, where all males were required to submit to military training at the age of 7 and join the army at 20 and stay until 30. Once they turn 30, they could vote and go home but stayed as members of the army until the age of 60. Girls were physically trained at an early age such as running, wrestling, gymnastics…
The government was Oligarchy headed by two kings who exercised strong control over the citizens with limited foreign entry and exit except for military reasons.

cards.title: Athens
body: Tyrant rule collapsed in Athens in the 6 B.C.E and was replaced by democracy. A council of 500 debated on the important issues. Under Pericles (5th C), Athens practiced direct democracy allowing everyone to participate in the assembly.
Every male participated in the general assembly made up of 43,000 adult males over 18 years old. While the women, slaves and non-citizens weren’t allowed in the assembly.

Religion- They were Polytheistic with hundreds of gods and goddesses, but they had 12 chief gods who they thought lived on Mount Olympus (highest mountain in Greece). Zeus was the chief god, Poseidon was the god of the sea, Ares was the god of war. Nike was the goddess of victory. Athena was the goddess of wisdom….
Philosophy- Philosophy in Greek means, love of wisdom. The greatest Greek philosophers were:

SOCRATES- is mostly known by his student Plato because he didn’t leave any written records. He taught for free using the Socratic Method (Q&A). He believed human bad behavior was resulted from ignorance and can be corrected through education. He criticized the Athenian government resulting in his death sentence, by poison.
PLATO- a student of Socrates who managed to write many books such as The Republic, where he wrote that a government headed by philosophers was the best type.

ARISTOTLE- studied at the Academy (Plato’s school in Athens) and wrote about politics, astronomy, biology, physics, studied the constitutions of 158 states and came up with the best government systems: Monarchy, Aristocracy, and Constitutional Government.

cards.title: Education, History, Drama and Art
body: Private education was made public during the Hellenistic period. Boys learned to read, write, music and athletics while girls learned to read, write and arithmetic. Greeks advanced in sciences such as Astronomy and Mathematics.

The Greeks were the first to write history in 5th B.C, Herodotus is the father of history. They were also the first writers of dramas and plays, most of which focused on tragedies. They excelled in architecture, sculpture, paintings, they built open air theatres, temples.

cards.title: Roman Civilization (500 B.C- 600 C.E)
body: Italy was the center of the Roman Civilization surrounded by sea and the Alps in the north.
1500-1000 B.C.E, Latin-speaking Indo-European groups moved to central Italy. After 800 B.C, two other groups moved to Italy, the Greeks, and Etruscans.

750-550 B.C, the Greeks moved to southern Italy and brought their culture with them while the Etruscans migrated from Asia Minor into northern Italy and transformed Rome from a village into a city. They had the biggest influence on the Roman Civilization.
Roman Civilization can be classified into two periods:

cards.title: Roman Republic
body: In 509 B.C, Romans overthrew the Etruscan monarchy and created a Republic (a government headed by a leader elected by the people).
Early Roman society was divided into Patricians (wealthy, landowning ruling class) and Plebeians (poor commoners). Both were considered citizens but only the Patricians voted.
Two consuls ran the government and the army, the Praetors oversaw civil law. The Senate was an assembly of 300 patricians who acted as advisors and made laws.

Intermarriage between the Patricians and the Plebeians was forbidden leading into a 100-year conflict where the Plebeians won. By 3 B.C, all males were made equal under the law while the wealthy dominated the society.

cards.title: Roman conquest of the Mediterranean
body: Roman expansion into the Mediterranean was challenged by the power of the Phoenician state of Carthage (Tunisia) as a challenge, resulting in the 3 Punic Wars (punicus is Latin for Phoenicians).

The First Punic War (264-241 B.C): broke out after Roman army reached Sicily that was under the Carthaginian Empire. The Romans built a strong navy and won, forcing Carthage to give up its claim over Sicily, making it a Roman province.

The Second Punic War (218-201 B.C): Carthage commander Hannibal attacked Spain with 46,000 troops, after both Italy and Spain tried to stop his expansion. He defeated the Romans despite the death of his soldiers while crossing the Alps. But the Romans reorganized in 206 B.C and pushed the Carthaginians out of Spain.

The Third Punic War (149-146 B.C): Romans set out to destroy Carthage. Within three years, they burnt the city, sold 50,000 people into slavery and plowed Carthage lands with salt making it a Roman province.
This victory enabled Romans to dominate western and eastern Mediterranean.

cards.title: Roman Empire
body: Romans faced internal problems: the growing inequality between the rich aristocrats and poor farmers, and the powerful military commanders leading into civil wars (82-31 B.C).

Julius Caesar was a powerful general in charge of the Roman army in Gaul (France), who entered Rome and controlled the government until his was killed by the Senate. Power struggle broke out after Caesar for 10 years until his nephew Octavian took power in 31 B.C.
Octavian was given the title Augustus (supreme leader) making the Rome an Empire. His reign from 31 B.C to 14 C.E is known as the Age of Augustus.

Pax Romana was a 100-year period of peace created by Augustus’s successors, during which the Roman Empire had 50 million people, and the good emperors begun massive building programs, tolerated foreigners, spread Roman culture mixed with Greek resulting in the Greco-Roman Civilization.

cards.title: Characteristic Features of the Roman Civilization – Economy, Society and Law
body: Agriculture was the chief occupation of most people.
Trade was conducted both with in the Empire and extended as far as China, Egypt. The flourishing trade helped the growth of manufacture.
A wide gap between the rich and poor, the rich lived in luxury and estates while the poor depended on the aristocrats for employment.

Families were Paterfamilias (patriarchal) putting the women under the absolute guardianship of the men and prohibiting them from education and the public life. Only the middle and upper-class women had some rights.
Roman society heavily depended on slave labor, even the poor farmers owned a few slaves. Greek slaves were used as tutors, musicians, doctors, and artists.
A law system of 12 tables was introduced in 450 B.C.E as a code of law for the farming society but was later improved to keep the peace and order of the Empire.

cards.title: Art, Architecture, Literature and Religion
body: 3rd - 2nd B.C, Romans adopted Greek art and architecture along with their own styles such as arches and domes. They were first to use concrete extensively to build roads, bridges, temples, and theatres because of their remarkable engineering skills.
During the Age of Augustus, Latin poetry and prose writing reached its height under the poets Virgil, Horace, historians such as Livy who wrote 142 books of Roman history.

They were polytheistic and worshipped many gods like Jupiter and Mars. The Senate officially declared Emperors as gods. Dramas, chariot races and gladiatorial shows were part of their religious festivals.

cards.title: The Rise of Christianity
body: Judea was a territory found in Palestine where the Jews lived. Following the appointment of Herod, the great (a Jew) by the Roman Senate as the king of Judea in 37 B.C, the land officially became part of the Roman Empire.

37 B.C- 26C.E, the Jews were engaged in fights with their neighbors while resisting the Roman heavy taxation. This created fear in the community which could only be eased with the coming of the Messiah (savor) as prophesized I the Bible.

Jesus was born in Nazareth and grew up to be a carpenter while learning the teachings of the Old Testament. He begun to preach among the Jews assisted by 12 apostles after he was baptized at the age of 30 by John the Baptist.
While some Jews followed his teachings, the Radical Jews opposed him because he didn’t help them fight against the Roman authority instead, he preached of humanity, love, and avoidance of violence.

Conservative Jews saw him as a false Messiah because he told them to correct their ways, while the Romans saw him as a potential leader of Jewish rebellion against the Empire. Jesus faced hostilities from all sides.
He was finally arrested by Jews in 33 C.E and was handed over to Pontius Pilate (Roman governor of Judea) who ordered the crucifixion.
The resurrection of Jesus witnessed by his disciples spread hope among the Jews and begun the spread of Christianity from Jerusalem.

cards.title: The Spread of Christianity
body: Christianity spread from Jerusalem to the whole world through Jesus’s disciples. Paul was one of them who was given the duty of spreading it throughout the Asia Minor and the Aegean Sea.
The teachings were passed orally at first, until they were written down in the form of Gospels (40-100 C.E). The Gospels were the foundation for the New Testament, the second part of the Bible.

By 100 C.E, Churches were established in the eastern part of Roman Empire. The spread of Christianity into the Empire was helped by the lack of attention from the leaders who thought it was another sect of Judaism.

With time, Roman tolerance faded, and they began to persecute the Christians throughout the first and second centuries. But Christianity had already taken root and spread extensively by the fourth century.

Constantine was the first Christian Roman Emperor who played the greatest role in legalizing Christianity by issuing the Edict of Milan in 313. The edict officially made Christianity a legal religion in the Roman Empire.
Emperor Theodosius (378-395) made Christianity the official religion of the Empire.

cards.title: The fall of the Roman Empire
body: Division of the Empire- in 395 the Empire was divided into west and east. Rome remained as the capital of the Western Roman Empire while Constantinople became the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire.
Economic Decline- Commerce declined over the years
Weak Emperors- weak and incapable leaders failed to preserve the power of the empire.
The Breakdown of communication- the growing gap between the two parts of the Empire resulted in the complete independence from each other and they lost contact.
The decline of public order- was resulted as the central authority was weakened due to weak rulers.
Invasion of German tribes (3rd C.E) - the Visigoths and Vandals were Germanic tribes who invaded the Western Roman Empire.

cards.title: Origin of the Eritrean People
body: The East African Great Rift Valley is believed to be the origin of humans. As part of the region, Eritrea has been home to most ancient humans according to the recent discovery of a 1-million-year-old hominid cranium found in Buya, northern Danakil Depression.

Eritrea had been occupied by hunter-gathering inhabitants for thousands of years. This known based on the prehistoric sites found in Aqordet, Qarora and Asmara. Rock Paintings found around Mai Ayni, Senafe, Sellum Ba’atti, Zeban Ona Lebanos…
The Eritrean society is the result of the interactions of pre-existing people with new immigrants that came in three waves.
The First Wave- Nilotic speaking group came from the Nile valley and settled in Gash Setit and some parts of the highlands
The Second Wave- Kushitic group came from southeast Egypt and northern Sudan, settled in Gash Barka, central highlands, and the coasts by pushing the Nilotic groups.
The Third Wave (1000-400 B.C) - Semitic groups (Sabeans) migrated from southern Arabia into the highland of Eritrea and Tigray.
Nilotic language group- Nara and Kunama
Cushitic language group- Hidareb, Bilen, Saho and Afar
Semitic language group- Tigrinya, Tigre and Rashaida (came in 19th C)

cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the three waves of migration that shaped Eritrean society, with today's language groups.

steps.text: First wave – Nilotic speakers from the Nile valley settled in Gash Setit and parts of the highlands (today Nara and Kunama).
Second wave – Kushitic groups from south-east Egypt and northern Sudan settled in Gash Barka, the central highlands and the coasts, pushing the Nilotic groups (today Hidareb, Bilen, Saho and Afar).
Third wave (1000–400 B.C.) – Semitic groups (Sabeans) from southern Arabia settled in the highlands of Eritrea and Tigray (today Tigrinya and Tigre; Rashaida came in the 19th century).
Conclude: Eritrean society came from the interaction of earlier inhabitants with these immigrants.

cards.answer: Nilotic (Nara, Kunama) → Kushitic (Hidareb, Bilen, Saho, Afar) → Semitic (Tigrinya, Tigre; later Rashaida).

cards.title: Ancient Eritrean Civilization
body: Eritrean ancient history has close relations with that of Egypt due to the Egyptian trade expeditions to the Land of Punt. Pictures in Egyptian temple, De’ir el-Bahr, show the connections the Pharaohs had with the people of the Red Sea coasts.
Ancient Eritrean history is classified into Pre-Aksumite and Aksumite periods
Pre-Aksumite Period; Ancient civilization existed in Eritrea long before the emergence of Aksum. Those pre-Aksumite civilizations developed farming, animal husbandry and social organization.

The Land of Punt emerged around 2500 B.C, it included the Eritrean coasts in the Red Sea. The area had extensive trade relations with Egypt and Phoenicia. Because the area was rich in gold, ivory and slaves, the Egyptians called it Punt, meaning the land of the gods.

The Da’amat Kingdom emerged during the 8th B.C, it was made up of the urban centers such as Adulis, Qohaito, Metera, Tekondae, Keskese and northern Tigray. Adulis was the Center and there was extensive trade with Greek, Roman Empire and Meroe.
Aksumite Period (1st -7th C.E); The Aksumite kingdom emerged out of the Da’amat, with the same urban centers. It was in present day Eritrea and northern Tigray.
The Periplus of the Erythrean Sea was a Greek guidebook in which Aksum was mentioned for the first time around 1 C.E.
The Empire reached its height during the 4th C, where the kings built massive stone steles to show their power.

cards.title: Economy
body: Maritime trade through the Port of Adulis was the main source of income. The Red Sea enabled trade with the Roman Empire, African and Arabian coasts and India. Gold, ivory, spices, and slaves were exchanged with iron weapons, clothes, wine and olive oil.
Trade was first conducted by barter until the beginning of coins in about 270 C.E. the coins were made of gold, silver, and bronze, they carried the names of the rulers.
The coins are important artifacts as they provide names and chronology of events.
The society depended agriculture, animal husbandry, crafts, metal works and pottery.

cards.title: The introduction of Christianity
body: One of the major developments of the 4th C in the Aksumite kingdom was the introduction of Christianity by Syrian missionaries in 330-340 C.E. before that, they were polytheistic and worshipped gods of the moon, sun…
4th C, two Syrian monks, Frumentius and Aedesius reached Aksum after sea waves wrecked their boat. They were invited into the court of the king where they converted king Ezana into Christianity.

The coming of nine saints in the 5th-6th century, led to the spread of Christianity over the region, and built the first monasteries such as the Abune Libanos Monastery (Senafe) with 1500 years old mummies.
Another major development was Aksumite conquest of Meroe under king Ezana.

cards.title: Decline
body: By the 6th C, Aksum became a major power in our region, it conquered Yemen in the name of protecting Christians from persecution. But begun to decline in the 7th C b/c
Persian conquest of Yemen and Arabia- Aksumite kingdom lost control over its sea routes. It also lost land trade routes in the Nile region due to the rise of a new state in Sudan, Soba.

The rise and expansion of Muslim Arabia in the Middle East and the Red Sea- around 700 C.E, Arabs controlled Adulis, the Red Sea, the Middle East and the Horn of Africa. They established the first Islamic state in 8th C, Dahlak Sultanate.

The migration and expansion of the Bejas in the 8th C- the Bejas settled along the borders of Egypt and northern Aksum. They occupied Massawa, Dahlak Islands, and Eritrean highlands and invaded the Aksumite Kingdom.
The kingdom grew weak and isolated because of the above-mentioned reasons and it finally collapsed in the 10th C.

steps.text: Maritime trade through the port of Adulis was the main source of income.
The Red Sea linked Aksum with the Roman Empire, African and Arabian coasts and India: gold, ivory, spices and slaves were exchanged for iron weapons, clothes, wine and olive oil.
