cards.title: Beja Expansion and the Spread of Islam
body: The Bejas expanded with the decline of the Aksumite Kingdom. They were Kushitic people who settled between Aswan (Sudan) and northwestern Eritrea in the 8th century. They expanded into Hirgigho, Sahel, Barka and Anseba valleys creating five independent kingdoms; the mining kingdoms of Naqis, Jarin, and Qat’a and the agriculturalists and pastoralist kingdoms of Bazin and Baqlin.
There are many stories and oral traditions about the Bejas in the Begattay Bilen tradition, Dina Fana and Belew Kelew of the highlands and the Rom of Sahel.
The Beja kingdoms disintegrated due to various wars in the 14th C.

cards.title: The Spread of Islam
body: The spread of Islam is a significant part of the Eritrean history because Eritrea was the first African country to accept Islam through Mohammed’s followers who crossed the Red Sea seeking refuge from the Qurayish tribe of Mecca in 615 C.E.

Up to the 10th C, the spread of Islam was limited to the Dahlak islands and the coasts of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden but the rise of the Fatimids in Egypt and the revival of Red Sea trade increased the expansion. Trade routes were the major channels of Islamic penetration into Eritrea.

The Dahlak Islands were annexed by Arabs in 8th C after the fall of the Aksumite kingdom and remained until the autonomous sultanate of Dahlak was established in 13th C. More than 200 written Arabic inscriptions were found in the island.

cards.title: Agew Migration
body: One of the earliest population movements in Eritrea that gave rise to the present day society was that of the Agew, Kushitic groups from Wag and Lasta (south of Tigray). The movement was caused after the center of the Aksumite kingdom shifted from Tigray to Wag and Lasta, forcing the inhabitants to move north into Eritrea.

During the 10th C, various Agew groups moved to Eritrea forming the present Bilen population. In the 13th C, another Agew group known as the Zagwe moved into the highlands and Anseba valley. The Zagwe were created under Queen Yodit, after she revolted against the Aksumites in the 12th C, but the Queen was overthrown by an Amhara ruler, Yekuno Amlak causing the migration of the Zagwe.

cards.title: Portuguese-Turkish Rivalry and the Gragn Wars
body: After the fall of Aksumite kingdom, Eritrea for the first time reappeared in the international scene in the 16th C as both the Turks and the Portuguese showed interest in the region. This was because they; wanted to control the strategically significant Red Sea, and the internal developments in Amhara-Tigray.

The war between the Christian highland state and the Islamic kingdom of Adal begun in the 14th C and reached its height during the 16th C with the rise of Ahmad Ibn Ibrahim (Gragn) as the sultan of Adal. Gragn wanted to end the war with the Christian state once and for all, thus build a large army by making alliances with Egypt and the Turks.
1529-1535, he defeated the Christians, overrun southern and northern Abyssinia and advanced towards the Eritrean highlands where he faced the forces of Bahri Negassi.

After his defeat, the Amhara king Libne Dengel asked the help of the Portuguese (since they were Christians). The Portuguese only accepted because of their previous geo-political interests in the Red Sea. Christopher Da Gamma led 400 troops from Goa (India) and landed at Massawa in 1541.

Galawdewos (Libne Dengel’s son) and the Portuguese scared Gragn into seeking the help of the Turk in Yemen. He received 900 troops and defeated the joint forces of Abyssinia and Portugal killing Da Gamma. Galawdewos conducted a surprise attack in 1543 killing Gragn and the sultanate collapsed.

cards.title: Bahri Negassi and the Turks
body: Bahri Negassi was a title given to the rulers of Midri Bahri (Eritrean highlands) with their capital at Debarwa. The rulers paid tribute to the Abyssinian Kings but had autonomous rule. Bahri Negassi Issak became autonomous after the fall of Gragn.

The Turks begun their expansionist projects in the Red Sea by occupying Saukin (Sudan) and Zeila (Somalia) and controlled Massawa and Hirghigo under Ozdemur Pasha in 1557 and moved towards the highlands, where they faced Issak.

Issak defeated the Turks and tried to overthrow King Minas (Abyssinian king). He sought an alliance with the Turks to defeat Minas and in return gave them Debarwa. Issak wasn’t happy with this alliance thus made agreements with Minas to remove the Turks from Debarwa in 1567.

Issak switched alliance with the Turks for the third time causing massive attacks from the Amhara king Sertse Dengil against him and the Turks in 1578. Sertse Dengel killed both Issak and the Pasha at the Battle of Adi Qoro, and destroyed the mosques in Debarwa. He tried to control Hirghigo but was defeated by the Turks,
In 1589 the Turks handed Massawa and Hirghigo over to the Naibs (local belew chiefs, representatives) to rule on their behalf.

cards.title: Impacts of Turkish Intervention in Eritrea (16th C)
body: They controlled the Eritrean coasts for about 300 years through the Naibs.
The Highlands were devastated by the constant wars between the Turks and the Amhara kings.
Turkish conquest started the first colonial era in Eritrea.
Turkish intervention gave rise to Bahri Negassi Issak.

cards.title: Social Changes and Population Movements (16th-17th C) – 1) Socio-economic changes in the central highlands
body: The Enda system was the common system of socio-economic organization in the highlands before the 16th C. The Enda was a large kinship group consisting large families with the common ancestor and a defined inherited land known as Risti. The system gave equal right.

16th C, Enda system begun to change due to the many migrations from Tigray and Ethiopia. Many old Endas formed into larger villages congregated into districts by the 17th C. Some districts include; Akkele Guzay, Seraye, Logochua, Shmezana, Qohain and Hamasien.
The Hazzega-Tza’azzega rivalry in Hamasien was one of the outstanding power struggles of the era.

Gulti was a new landownership system, it was one of the economic changes of that time along with the social differences between those with the right to own land (Restenyatat) and those with no Risti or who aren’t originally from the village they live in (Ma’ekelay Aliet). Only the Restenyatat were alowed to participate in village administration.

After the death of Issak, Amhara Kings created military garrisons in Eritrea and also provided land grants to churches and monasteries. Gulti land was also granted to royal officials. The Gulti system didn’t replace the Risti system though.

cards.title: 2) Western Lowlands
body: In the northwestern part, the Beja and Tigre formed a loose confederation known as the Beni Amir Confederation. At the same time, the Funj (Sudanese kingdom), formed in the 16th C in the Nile valley, expanded into those areas. The funj were pastoralists and horsemen with their center at Sennar.

The funj rules the lands indirectly through the Nabtabs, who were the ruling class of the Beni Amir who collected tribute for the Funj. The Diglal was the chief of the Nabtabs and his deputy was the Sheikh al-Mashaikh. The job of the Shiekh was providing religious guidance to the Diglal.

The Nabtabs has a master-serf relationship with the Tigre. The Tigre served the Nabtabs by herding their cattle and domestic services. Intermarriage between the Nabtabs and the Serfs was prohibited, this continued until the 1940s.

The Nara and the Kunama were egalitarian communities who belonged to the same linguistic family and culture. They depended on farming and animal husbandry. 16th -17th C, Amhara and Tigray kings raided and killed thousands of the Nara and Kunama reducing their size.

cards.title: 3. Coastal Plains and Escarpmet
body: The eastern lowlands covered Semhar and Dankalia, were under the rule of the Turks, including the groups of Saho, Afar and Tigre.

The Saho were organized into equal clans with democratically elected elders. The Afar had a stratified society with rigid distinction between the upper and lower classes. They later established sultanates in Rahaita, Beilul and Assab.

cards.title: 4. Northern Highlands, Sahel and Senhit
body: The Bet Asghede were from Tsnadegle (Akkel Guzay), they came to Addi Nefas (Hamassien). In the 17th C, they moved to Sahel and gave rise to the Habab and Adi Temariam there. They became the masters of the indigenous people there.
16th -17th C, the Bet Tawqe (Bilen speaking group) moved fro the Hamasien region to Keren followed by another group the Bet Tarke.

cards.title: Tigrean Expansion into Eritrea (18th -19th C)
body: By the end of the 18th C, the decline of the Amhara government gave rise to regional feudal lords who used their fiefs as their main source of income. This period is known as the ‘Era of Princes’ or Zemene Measafinti.
The Tigrean lords thought that by controlling Eritrea they would
Collect taxes and tributes from the Eritreans
Get access to the coasts to conduct arms trade
Benefit from the Red Sea trade

The rivalry between the Bahri Negestat and the Niabs gave the Tigreans a chance to expand into Eritrea without much resistance. Some tigrean and Amhara lords include; Rasi Michael Sehul, Rasi Woldeselsie, Deiat Sbabgadis, Ras Wubie of semien and Ras Alula. They pillaged and killed many Eritreans and forced them to pay taxes. The Nara and Kumana were devastated as two thirds of them were killed.

cards.title: Egyptian and Tigrai- Amhara rivalry over Eritrea (2nd half of the 19th C)
body: 19th C, countries like Abyssinia, Egypt, France and Britain tried to control Eritrea. But the most notable one were the attempts from Tigrai-Amhara and Egypt.

The Ottoman rule in the coasts begun to decline in the 19th C, while Egypt grew powerful under Mohammad Ali. In his attempts to control the African coasts, he invaded Sudan in 1821 and Massawa by making arrangements with the Ottomans in 1846-1849. Mohammad’s expansion into the highlands was stopped by the Tigreans and Amharas in the area.

1870, Khedive Ismail Pasha planned to annex Eritrea with Sudan. He sent the Swiss mercenary Muzinger Pasha to Bogos in 1872, who was accepted by the people who were tired of Tigray raids. Egypt sent 3 forces to the highlands under

They occupied Asmara and Adi Quala under Coloniel Ahrendrup, Mereb in 1875 where they faced the forces of Emperor Yohannes who defeated the Egyptians at the Battle of Gundet. Muzinger was defeated and killed by the Afars. The third force defeated the Amir of Harar and controlled Harar.

1876, Khedive Ismail marched towards the highlands with a large army and fought the Battle of Gurae with the Abyssinan forces. He lost and the Egyptians retreated back to the coasts, where they remained until the coming of the Italians in 1885.

cards.title: Highland Rivalry
body: During the Egyptian attempts into the Eritrean highlands, Woledemichael Solomon of Hazzega, joined Emperor Yohannes against the Egyptians. He captured 700 rifles at the battle of Gundet and in return, was given the title Degiat and recognized as the highland ruler by Yohannes.

Later, Woldemichael disagreed with Yohannes when he refused to hand over the rifles he captured from the Egyptians. Woldemichael sided with the Egyptians who gave him the title Rasi. In retaliation, Yohannes sided with Deiat Hailu of Tseazzega. A battle followed in 1877 and Woldemichael defeated Hailu at the Battle of Woki Dubba.

Yohannes was afraid of Woldemichael and sent his army to disarm him, but Woldemichael defeated him at the Battle near Asmara in 1878. Yohannes sent Ras Alula to trick Woldemichael, who went to Tigray with him because he was promised safety. But when they reached Tigray, Woldemichael was arrested. He died a year later in 1905.
The death of Woldemichael created an opportunity for the Tigreans to control Eritrea until the coming of the Italians.

body: Gave way to Tirgray expansion
Continuous wars resulted in the destruction of villages, people and property.

questions.label: 20. Where are prehistoric rock paintings found in Eritrea?

options.A: Around Mai Ayni, Senafe and Sellum Ba'atti

why: Answer A: Around Mai Ayni, Senafe and Sellum Ba'atti
The lesson lists rock paintings around Mai Ayni, Senafe, Sellum Ba'atti and Zeban Ona Lebanos.
Prehistoric sites are also found in Aqordet, Qarora and Asmara.
They show hunter-gatherers lived in Eritrea for thousands of years.
